content: A cube is a three-dimensional solid object characterized by six square faces, with three faces meeting at each vertex. It is also known as a regular hexahedron and is one of the five Platonic solids. The cube is a specific type of square prism, rectangular parallelepiped, and a three-sided trapezohedron. It is geometrically dual to the octahedron and exhibits cubic symmetry, also referred to as octahedral symmetry. The cube represents the three-dimensional case of the broader concept of a hypercube, which can exist in any number of dimensions. For a cube centered at the origin in Cartesian coordinates, with edges parallel to the axes and an edge length of 2, the vertices are defined by specific coordinate points. The interior of the cube consists of all points (x₀, x₁, x₂) where -1 < xᵢ < 1. The volume of a cube with edge length (a) is calculated as (a^3), which is why third powers are referred to as cubes, analogous to squares and second powers. Among cuboids (rectangular boxes) with a given surface area, the cube has the largest volume. Similarly, for cuboids with the same total linear size (length + width + height), the cube also maximizes volume. The cube has three classes of symmetry, which can be represented by vertex-transitive coloring of its faces. The highest symmetry, octahedral symmetry ((O_h)), involves all faces being the same color. Dihedral symmetry ((D_{4h})) arises from the cube being a prism, with four side faces sharing the same color. The lowest symmetry ((D_{2h})) is also prismatic, with alternating colors on the side faces, resulting in three colors paired by opposite sides. Each symmetry class corresponds to a distinct Wythoff symbol. The cube is unique among Platonic solids in its ability to tile space regularly. It is also the only Platonic solid with faces that have an even number of sides, making it a zonohedron (a polyhedron where every face exhibits point symmetry). In four-dimensional Euclidean space, the cube's analogue is called a tesseract or, less commonly, a hypercube. In (n)-dimensional Euclidean space, the generalization of the cube is referred to as an (n)-dimensional hypercube or simply (n)-cube, also known as a measure polytope. Lower-dimensional analogues of the cube include a point in zero dimensions, a line segment in one dimension, and a square in two dimensions. The vertices of a cube can be grouped into two sets of four, each forming a regular tetrahedron. Together, these tetrahedra create a regular compound known as the stella octangula. The intersection of these two tetrahedra forms a regular octahedron. The symmetries of a regular tetrahedron correspond to those of a cube that map each tetrahedron onto itself, while the remaining cube symmetries map the two tetrahedra onto each other. One such tetrahedron has a volume equal to one-third of the cube's volume. The remaining space within the cube is divided into four equal irregular polyhedra, each with a volume of one-sixth of the cube's volume. The rectified cube is known as the cuboctahedron. By truncating smaller corners of the cube, a polyhedron with six octagonal faces and eight triangular faces can be obtained. In particular, regular octagons can be achieved, resulting in a truncated cube. The rhombicuboctahedron is formed by cutting off both corners and edges of the cube to the correct extent. A cube can also be inscribed within a dodecahedron such that each vertex of the cube coincides with a vertex of the dodecahedron, and each edge of the cube aligns with a diagonal of one of the dodecahedron's faces. Collectively, all such cubes form the regular compound of five cubes. The cube graph is a combinatorial representation of the cube, consisting of its vertices and edges. It is a specific case of the hypercube graph. An extension of this concept is the three-dimensional (k)-ary Hamming graph, which, for (k = 2), corresponds to the cube graph. Such graphs are significant in the theory of parallel processing in computer systems.
